newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore output slumps surprise 7.6 pct in August.
newsitem.headline: Singapore output slumps surprise 7.6 pct in August.

text.p: Singapore's total manufacturing output fell an unexpected 7.6 percent year-on-year in August due to a slowdown in the country's core electronics industry, the Economic Development Board (EDB) said on Monday.
The city-state's production of chemicals, transport equipment, plastic and petroleum products also declined, the EDB said in a statement.
Economists said the data were worse than expected, and some said they might adjust downwards their forecast for the country's overall economic growth for the year to reflect the poor August figures.
The EDB said Singapore's cumulative growth for manufacturing in the first eight months of 1996 was 6.4 percent.
Singapore's economy has been badly affected by a worldwide slump in demand for electronics, due to its heavy dependence on this sector.
Electronics and related products accounted for almost half the country's industrial output and about 60 percent of its non-oil exports in 1995.
But the latest data show the general economic slowdown appears to have spread further than the electronics industry.
The paint, pharmaceuticals and chemicals industry was one of the worst affected sectors, registering a 24.6 percent decline in output year-on-year.
Production of transport equipment fell 18.5 percent while output of plastic products declined 15.5 percent, the EDB said.
"We were anticipating a bad figure, but this was worse than we could have predicted," said Chia Woon Khien, economist at UBS Securities in Singapore.
"It shows the economic slowdown has spread out from electronics to the other sectors, particularly to petroleum refining and chemicals."
She said UBS would now review its forecast for growth in Singapore's gross domestic product (GDP) for 1996 as a whole.
"We were predicting growth for the economy to be between seven and eight percent this year...I think it could now hit below seven percent," she said.
Stock market analysts also greeted the August production figure with a mixture of dismay and resignation.
"We're not done yet with negative statistics," said Lim Eng Hai, director of research at local brokerage J.M. Sassoon.
"Singapore's economy is closely tied to the electronics industry and it is clear people have been cutting costs across the board," he said.
"But the slowdown won't last indefinitely...We are looking for a recovery in the first quarter of 1997."
